basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: What is an import?
back: A good or service bought from another country.

base_cards.front: What does a population pyramid show?
back: The age and sex structure of a population.

base_cards.front: Define immigration.
back: Movement into a country to live.

base_cards.front: What is suburbanisation?
back: Movement of people or activities from the inner city to the urban edge.

base_cards.front: Name one indicator of development within the UK.
back: Income.

base_cards.front: Which city is the major UK city case study in this course?
back: Leeds.

base_cards.front: Explain why using income alone may give a misleading picture of development.
back: Income does not show health, education or access to services.
An average can hide large differences between people or neighbourhoods.

base_cards.front: Give two reasons why an area with good infrastructure may attract businesses.
back: Transport links make workers, customers and goods easier to reach.
Reliable broadband helps firms communicate and provide digital services.

base_cards.front: Explain why the UK population is ageing.
back: People live longer because death rates have fallen.
Lower birth rates mean young people form a smaller share of the population.

base_cards.front: Give one social and one economic benefit of immigration.
back: Social: migrants can add cultural diversity.
Economic: migrants can fill skills gaps, work and pay taxes.

base_cards.front: Explain one possible consequence of counter-urbanisation for a rural settlement.
back: Housing demand may rise as people move in.
This can increase prices and make homes less affordable for existing residents.

base_cards.front: Give two challenges created by rapid city growth.
back: Increased demand for affordable housing.
More congestion and pressure on transport.

base_cards.front: Explain one reason why development varies across the UK.
back: Areas with poor transport or digital connections are less accessible.
Firms may invest elsewhere because costs or travel times are lower.
This reduces job opportunities and income in the less connected area.

base_cards.front: Explain one challenge caused by an ageing population.
back: A larger older population increases demand for healthcare and social care.
These services require more workers and public spending.
With fewer workers per dependent person, funding them can become harder.

base_cards.front: Explain how migration can change the character of a city.
back: Migrants bring languages, food, beliefs and traditions.
They may establish businesses and community services.
These changes make neighbourhoods and the city's workforce more diverse.

base_cards.front: Explain how the decline of the docks affected Salford Quays.
back: Larger container ships and competition from coastal ports reduced dock activity.
The docks closed in 1982, removing dock and linked industrial jobs.
Unemployment, polluted water and derelict land damaged the area's environment and image.

base_cards.front: Explain how government policy and infrastructure can reduce uneven development.
back: Government can fund regeneration, education or business support in weaker areas.
These policies can create jobs and improve skills.
Better roads, rail and broadband connect people and firms to markets.
Improved accessibility can attract investment and raise incomes.

base_cards.front: Explain two possible impacts of re-urbanisation.
back: Reusing brownfield land can bring homes, jobs and improved public spaces back to an inner city.
Rising demand may increase rents and house prices, so some lower-income residents may be displaced or excluded.

base_cards.front: Explain how regeneration changed Salford Quays.
back: Public investment reclaimed land, cleaned the waterfront and improved transport and public space.
The Lowry opened in 2000 and MediaCity in 2011, attracting visitors, broadcasters and creative firms.
MediaCity now contains major broadcasters and more than 250 creative and technology businesses.
However, expensive housing and skilled jobs mean benefits are not shared equally with nearby communities.

base_cards.front: Explain why Leeds is important at more than one scale.
back: Leeds had about 812,000 residents in 2021 and around 471,000 people work there, making it a major regional employment and service centre.
Finance, retail, healthcare, universities and culture attract people from across northern England.
Rail and motorway links connect firms and workers to other UK cities.
Universities and internationally connected businesses also attract overseas students, skills and investment.

updates.front: Name one indicator of development within the UK.
back: Income, life expectancy, educational attainment, employment or broadband access can help compare opportunities and living conditions. Ethnicity describes diversity, rather than a higher-to-lower development ranking.

additions.front: Why can the UK import and export cars at the same time?
back: Different firms produce different models and components. Trade is not limited to one country making everything in a broad product category.

additions.front: Which was the UK’s largest individual trading partner for goods and services in 2025?
back: The United States, with about 17.5% of total trade. The scope includes both exports and imports of goods and services.

additions.front: Why should a goods-only trade ranking not be treated as a total-trade ranking?
back: Total trade includes services as well as goods. Including finance, consultancy and other services can change the order of partners.

additions.front: Give an example of a tertiary and a quaternary job.
back: A shop worker provides a tertiary service. A research scientist or software-research specialist performs quaternary, knowledge-based work.

additions.front: Can manufacturing employment fall while a factory’s output stays high?
back: Yes. Automation and productivity improvements can reduce the workers needed to produce the same or a larger amount.

additions.front: Why is ethnicity not a measure for ranking how developed a population is?
back: It describes cultural identity and diversity. It does not place ethnic groups on a higher-to-lower development scale.

additions.front: Why can average regional income hide local deprivation?
back: A high average can be raised by wealthy residents while other neighbourhoods have low incomes. Living costs and the distribution of income also matter.

additions.front: How can a factory closure create a negative multiplier effect?
back: Workers lose earnings and spend less locally. Suppliers and nearby shops lose income too, which can cause further job losses.

additions.front: Why might regeneration jobs not automatically benefit former dock workers?
back: The new roles may require different skills, qualifications or access. Training and affordable transport help connect existing residents to opportunities.

additions.front: When did the docks close at Salford Quays, and why is that useful evidence?
back: They closed in 1982. It anchors the explanation of job loss, dereliction and the later need for regeneration.

additions.front: Were the original MediaCity figures of 10,000 jobs and £1 billion measured completed outcomes?
back: No. They were early projections for economic growth. They should be described as forecasts rather than proof that every outcome had happened.

additions.front: Why can a country’s total population grow when deaths exceed births?
back: Positive net migration can outweigh natural decrease. Total change combines natural change with migration.

additions.front: What is one important difference between a population pyramid and the DTM?
back: A pyramid shows age and sex structure. The DTM describes changes in birth and death rates through broad stages.

additions.front: Why is later retirement not equally suitable for every older person?
back: Health, caring responsibilities and the physical demands of work differ. The policy can increase labour supply but may be harder for some groups.

additions.front: Do the 2025 study and work immigration percentages describe every UK immigrant?
back: No. The 47% study and 23% work figures refer to the specified non-EU+ group in that year. They should not be applied to all arrivals.

additions.front: How does re-urbanisation differ from counter-urbanisation?
back: Re-urbanisation brings people and investment back to inner urban areas. Counter-urbanisation moves people from cities to smaller settlements or rural areas.

additions.front: What does Leeds West Indian Carnival illustrate about migration?
back: Migration can shape culture, leisure and the use of public space, as well as population numbers. The carnival began in 1967.

additions.front: Why is the Leeds PIPES network more specific evidence than simply saying a city recycles?
back: It uses recovered heat to supply buildings, linking waste treatment to lower-carbon heating. Its value depends on actual connections, operation and who benefits.
